name: Translating Akkadian to English with neural machine translation (PNAS Nexus 2(5), pgad096); the model is also publicised as the 'Babylonian Engine', with code released on GitHub as Akkademia
date: Received 10 August 2022; accepted 8 March 2023; published 2 May 2023 (PNAS Nexus, vol. 2, issue 5)
creator: Gai Gutherz (School of Computer Science, Tel Aviv University), Shai Gordin (Digital Pasts Lab, Ariel University), Luis Sáenz (Ariel University and Heidelberg University), Omer Levy and Jonathan Berant (Tel Aviv University)
form: Peer-reviewed research article plus an open-source neural machine translation model (convolutional sequence-to-sequence network built with Fairseq) and code
effect_on_arc: None directly. The model recovered no new Gilgamesh text and was not tested on the epic. Its relevance is methodological: it shows how far machine translation gets with formulaic Akkadian and how badly it does with literary Akkadian, which is the register Gilgamesh is written in
critical_response: Widely covered in 2023 (Times of Israel, Decrypt, ZME Science, Language Log). Coverage stressed the headline BLEU4 score of about 37 and the claim of translation close to a novice human level. Language Log noted that Google Translate scores around 60 BLEU for Spanish to English, putting the result in perspective. Assyriologist Nathan Wasserman (Hebrew University), quoted in the Times of Israel, said that 'for deeper and less formulaic texts, this is still very far from being useful' and that having the words right 'doesn't mean you understand'. The authors themselves frame it as a tool to assist scholars and students, not a replacement
controversies: No dispute over the paper's honesty; the authors report their own weaknesses. The debate is about hype: headlines such as 'AI translates 5,000-year-old cuneiform at the push of a button' overstated a model that works best on repetitive royal inscriptions and administrative letters and produces 'total hallucinations' (fluent English unrelated to the source) on literary and unfamiliar texts. BLEU as a measure of translation quality for poetry is itself questionable, and the training data (ORACC translations) encode the choices of the human translators who made them
regional_reception: An Israeli academic project (Tel Aviv and Ariel universities). Ariel University is located in a West Bank settlement, which has drawn academic-boycott criticism of the institution generally [uncertain: no specific boycott response to this paper found]. No evidence found of Iraqi or Kurdish reception of this work
method: Machine translation. A convolutional neural network (Fairseq CNN encoder-decoder) trained on parallel Akkadian-English sentences from ORACC projects (RINAP, RIAo, RIBo, SAAo, Suhu). Two tasks: cuneiform Unicode signs straight to English (C2E) and Latin-script transliteration to English (T2E). Compared against a translation-memory baseline; evaluated with BLEU4 plus human review by Assyriologists of the error types
ai_pipeline_stage: Translation (the final step, after a tablet has been read into Unicode signs or transliteration by a human or another model)
scale_metrics: 8,056 texts; about 56,160 sentences for T2E and 50,299 for C2E. BLEU4: 37.47 (T2E) and 36.52 (C2E), versus translation-memory baselines of 23.51 and 27.09. Best on royal decrees and inscriptions, administrative letters and astrological/divination reports (mainly first millennium BCE Neo-Assyrian and Neo-Babylonian material); worst on legal transactions, literary texts and Old Babylonian texts. Quality drops for sentences over about 118 characters. Over half a million cuneiform tablets are thought to exist, most untranslated
what_was_found: No text or object. The contribution is a working translation tool and a measurement of where machine translation of Akkadian succeeds (formulaic genres) and where it fails (literature, names, broken lines). The paper tests an unknown passage from the Epic of Erra, a Babylonian poem, as an example of literary difficulty
provenance_and_ethics: Training data come from ORACC, an open, openly licensed scholarly corpus of translations made by Assyriologists [uncertain: licence detail]. The model and code are published on GitHub (Akkademia). The paper handles no physical objects. Ethical issues are second-order: the model inherits the biases and word choices of existing (mostly Western) translations, and fluent hallucinated output could mislead non-specialists
ai_craft_tension: This is the clearest contrast with Simon Armitage's Gilgamesh. Armitage cannot read Akkadian and works from a literal crib by Assyriologist Jacob Dahl, then turns it into verse. The Gutherz model does the crib step: it turns signs into rough literal English, and does it well only where the Akkadian is repetitive and formulaic (royal boasts, reports, letters). On literary texts it hallucinates, producing confident, fluent English that has nothing to do with the tablet. That is precisely the failure a poet must never commit and a scholar exists to catch. The machine can triage a backlog of hundreds of thousands of administrative tablets; it cannot yet produce a trustworthy crib of an epic, and it has no notion of what a line should sound like, why a gap matters or which version to follow. Human judgement stays at both ends: the Assyriologist who checks the literal sense and the poet who decides what it means in English
essay_hooks: (1) Gai Gutherz: 'What's so amazing about it is that I don't need to understand Akkadian at all to translate' (Times of Israel, 2023). Set this beside Armitage, who also cannot read Akkadian but relies on a human expert. (2) Nathan Wasserman: 'For deeper and less formulaic texts, this is still very far from being useful' and 'even when you have the words correct, it doesn't mean you understand' (Times of Israel). (3) BLEU score about 37 for Akkadian versus about 60 for Google's Spanish to English (Language Log). (4) Literary texts produced 'total hallucinations': fluent English unrelated to the source. A machine version of smoothing over a gap. (5) Trained on roughly 50,000 sentences, a tiny corpus by modern AI standards, against over half a million surviving tablets. (6) The model is best at kings bragging and officials reporting, the least poetic Akkadian there is. Gilgamesh is exactly where it breaks down
